{
  "title": "LocoMimicGen: Coupled SE(3) Object-Centric Demo Multiplication for Mobile Humanoid Loco-Manipulation",
  "core_problem": "How can a handful of expensive teleoperated whole-body loco-manipulation demonstrations be multiplied by orders of magnitude across diverse spatial configurations — new object positions, table heights, room obstacle layouts — while maintaining physical validity for the mobile bipedal humanoid platform? Isaac Lab's 2.3 GA release contains three directly relevant prior contributions. PR #3150 (merged Sept 9, 2025) adds the G1 loco-manipulation environment integrating a pretrained RL locomotion policy with Pink IK arm control. PR #3259 ('Adds locomanipulation data generation via disjoint navigation', merged Sept 10, 2025) adds pick-navigate-place phase segmentation with occupancy-map path planning between phases and scene randomization of tabletop positions, navigation destinations, and floor obstacles — making it the closest structural predecessor to LocoMimicGen. PR #3992 (merged Dec 1, 2025) extends the Mimic framework with a 'body end-effector' API and navigation controller integration. Despite this infrastructure, three technical gaps prevent room-level combinatorial scaling: PR #3259 handles navigation 'disjointly' — the manipulation stance (where the robot stands to manipulate) is fixed from the source demo and navigation is handled as path-level occupancy-map planning between fixed phases, NOT as coupled SE(3) object-centric encoding of stances jointly with arm trajectories. None of these PRs enforce arm-reachability constraints on base-pose selection during retargeting — the robot manipulates from whatever stance the source demo used, regardless of arm workspace feasibility for new object positions. And none perform combinatorial composition of subtask segments from multiple source demonstrations. These three absences cap achievable diversity at object-position randomization within a single source demo's reach envelope, rather than the combinatorial room-level scaling that MimicGen achieves for tabletop tasks.",
  "opportunity": "Isaac Lab's 2.3 GA release (PRs #3150, #3259, #3992) now provides the exact scaffolding — G1 environment, pick-navigate-place phase segmentation, occupancy-map path planning, Mimic segmentation framework, and navigation controller integration — needed to build a principled extension. The precise technical gap is narrow but high-impact: adding (1) SE(3) object-centric encoding of navigation stances jointly with arm trajectories into the existing Mimic segment representation (replacing the disjoint path-planning approach of PR #3259 with coupled frame-transform retargeting), (2) stance-conditioned reachability-map-guided base-pose optimization enforcing arm feasibility at each manipulation stance during retargeting (adapting IRM methodology from the mobile-manipulator literature to the bipedal humanoid setting, where the reachability map is conditioned on whole-body configuration rather than just SE(2) base pose), and (3) combinatorial subtask segment composition from multiple source demonstrations. OmniRetarget (Amazon, Sept 2025) and ULTRA (arXiv:2603.03279, March 2026) address humanoid loco-manipulation data generation via physics-preserving retargeting of MoCap sequences onto the G1, but retarget continuous motion sequences and cannot combinatorially compose segments across scene variants. DemoHLM (Oct 2025) demonstrates generalizable single-demonstration adaptation across 10 G1 loco-manipulation household tasks but the single-demo paradigm limits scaling to spatial interpolation within one source demo's envelope. The three-part Isaac Lab Mimic extension proposed here is tractable within existing infrastructure, precisely bounded against Isaac Lab's own 2.3 baseline (including PR #3259 as the most direct predecessor), and is the missing ingredient for room-level combinatorial scaling. MoMaGen (ICLR 2026, arXiv:2510.18316) imposes reachability as a hard constraint for wheeled bimanual mobile base-pose sampling — SE(2) for a wheeled platform. Now peer-reviewed at ICLR 2026, MoMaGen's coverage of hard-reachability-constrained demo generation makes the bipedal differentiation the critical point of departure: MoMaGen's reachability constraint operates over SE(2) base pose for a wheeled bimanual platform where the base pose fully determines arm workspace, whereas LocoMimicGen's stance-conditioned IRM addresses the qualitatively harder bipedal case where arm reachability is conditioned on whole-body configuration — COM height, foot contact, balance state — a higher-dimensional reachability function not covered by any prior data-generation work. EgoHumanoid (OpenDriveLab, arXiv:2602.10106, Feb 2026) and Ψ₀ (Physical Superintelligence Lab, arXiv:2603.12263, March 2026) represent concurrent human-data-driven paradigms — co-training VLA policies on human egocentric video alongside robot demonstrations — that highlight the orthogonal value of LocoMimicGen's combinatorial simulation synthesis approach.",
  "landscape": "MimicGen (CoRL 2023) decomposes arm demonstrations into object-centric subtask segments and applies SE(3) frame transformations — manipulation-only. DexMimicGen (ICRA 2025) extends this to bimanual dexterous humanoids, still tabletop. HumanoidGen (NeurIPS 2025) uses LLM-driven planning for tabletop dexterous tasks with 120+ scene variants — explicitly excludes locomotion. SoftMimicGen (arXiv:2603.25725, March 2026) extends MimicGen to deformable object manipulation on single-arm, bimanual, humanoid, and surgical platforms — strictly tabletop, no locomotion component. DemoGen (arXiv:2502.16932, RSS 2025) generates spatially augmented demonstrations from one human-collected demonstration per task via TAMP-style trajectory decomposition and 3D point-cloud visual synthesis — tabletop manipulation, with a whole-body controller used only for execution on mobile platforms, not for loco-manipulation data generation per se. Neither SoftMimicGen nor DemoGen addresses coupled SE(3) locomotion-stance encoding, stance-conditioned IRM for bipedal humanoids, or combinatorial multi-source segment composition.

Isaac Lab 2.3 loco-manipulation infrastructure comprises three PRs that together form the primary baseline. PR #3150 (merged Sept 9, 2025) adds Isaac-PickPlace-Locomanipulation-G1-Abs-v0, integrating a pretrained RL locomotion policy (velocity commands vx, vy, wz) with Pink IK arm control, achieving 92% success on pick-and-place. PR #3259 ('Adds locomanipulation data generation via disjoint navigation', merged Sept 10, 2025, release/2.3.0) is the closest structural predecessor to LocoMimicGen: it adds pick-navigate-place phase segmentation, occupancy-map-based collision-free path planning between phases, and scene randomization of tabletop object positions, navigation destinations, and floor obstacles. The implementation lives under disjoint_navigation/ and works by (a) recording static manipulation teleoperation with the base stationary, (b) applying Mimic augmentation to manipulation segments, and (c) stitching path-planned navigation trajectories between the resulting phases. Critically, PR #3259 does NOT encode navigation stances in the object's SE(3) local frame — navigation is occupancy-map path planning at the trajectory level, while the manipulation stance (where the robot stands to manipulate) is fixed from the source demo, not retargeted to new object positions. There is no arm-reachability constraint on base-pose selection: if a new object position falls outside the arm workspace at the source demo's stance, the generation produces infeasible trajectories rather than finding a feasible stance. There is no combinatorial composition from multiple source demonstrations. PR #3992 (merged Dec 1, 2025) adds a 'body end-effector' API and get_navigation_state() integration into the Mimic framework but relies on the same state-based navigation repetition/skipping, not object-centric stance encoding.

Inverse reachability maps (IRM) for robot base placement are a well-established technique. Vahrenkamp et al. 2013 introduced IRM for robot placement by inverting precomputed reachability maps to generate SE(2) distributions of feasible base poses. Burget et al. (ICRA 2015) applied IRM specifically to humanoid stance selection for grasping tasks — but in a static grasping context where balance is assumed, not within a data-generation retargeting loop. MoMa-Pos (arXiv:2403.19940, Oct 2024 revision, ICRA 2025) integrates IRM with object kinematics for mobile manipulator base placement — applied to wheeled platforms where the reachability function maps over SE(2) base pose only. MoMaGen (ICLR 2026, arXiv:2510.18316) imposes reachability as a hard constraint for wheeled bimanual mobile base-pose sampling — again, SE(2) for a wheeled platform. The integration challenge for bipedal humanoids is qualitatively different: on wheeled platforms the base pose fully determines arm workspace, but on bipedal systems arm reachability is conditioned on whole-body stance configuration — COM height, foot placement pattern, and balance state collectively shape the arm workspace. A concurrent planning paper (Murooka et al., arXiv:2505.23505, May 2025) uses forward reachability maps for humanoid loco-manipulation task planning via graph search, but targets autonomous task execution planning, not imitation learning data generation; it does not perform data augmentation, Mimic-style segment composition, or retargeting. The same CNRS-AIST group (Murooka et al., arXiv:2508.11275, Humanoids 2025) subsequently introduced learned differentiable reachability maps for optimization-based humanoid motion generation — continuous scalar-valued functions differentiable with respect to task-space coordinates, enabling gradient-based planning for footstep sequencing and loco-manipulation without repeated IK solving. The differentiable formulation excels at online continuous optimization but is not suited to LocoMimicGen's batch data-generation context: evaluating differentiable map gradients across 2048+ parallel Isaac Lab environments at retargeting time would bottleneck generation throughput, whereas LocoMimicGen's offline-precomputed discrete IRM is evaluated as a table lookup simultaneously across all environments. The two approaches are complementary in use case — differentiable maps for online planning, discrete IRM for batch generation — and both leave the stance-conditioned data-generation problem unaddressed.

OmniRetarget (Amazon, arXiv:2509.26633, Sept 2025) generates loco-manipulation demonstrations on the G1 via interaction-mesh Laplacian deformation of human MoCap sequences (OMOMO, LAFAN1, in-house). It preserves spatial and contact relationships and enables augmentation across embodiments, terrains, and object configurations. ULTRA (Xialin He et al., arXiv:2603.03279, March 2026) similarly scales whole-body loco-manipulation via physics-driven neural retargeting of large-scale MoCap to humanoid embodiments while preserving physical plausibility for contact-rich interactions, additionally learning a unified multimodal controller for autonomous goal-conditioned operation from egocentric perception. Both OmniRetarget and ULTRA (a) require large MoCap databases rather than small teleoperated G1 demonstrations; (b) retarget continuous motion sequences without decomposing into reusable subtask segments; (c) cannot combinatorially compose segments from different source demos; and (d) do not address the manipulation-stance feasibility problem for new object positions. OmniRetarget's codebase (Holosoma, amazon-far/holosoma) is publicly available; LocoMimicGen positions both as conceptual comparisons citing published retargeting fidelity metrics, as the estimated 10–14 day setup cost for Holosoma plus MoCap dataset ingestion exceeds the available bandwidth in the 20-day window.

DemoHLM (arXiv:2510.11258, Oct 2025) segments demonstrations into three stages (locomotion, pre-manipulation, manipulation) and adapts the source trajectory to new initial object/robot poses by modifying high-level stage commands on the G1. It demonstrates 10 loco-manipulation household tasks with sim-to-real transfer. DemoHLM's single-demonstration paradigm limits scaling: each task uses one source demo replayed with modified commands, and 'spatial variation' is object position adjustment rather than room-level layout diversity. DemoHLM's code has not been publicly released as of May 2026; LocoMimicGen therefore positions it as a conceptual comparison, citing its published 10-task evaluation results directly.

MoMaGen (ICLR 2026, arXiv:2510.18316) generates bimanual mobile manipulation demonstrations via constrained optimization (hard reachability + soft visibility) on a wheeled bimanual mobile base. The wheeled platform decouples navigation from balance, making MoMaGen's SE(2) base-pose sampling inapplicable to bipedal humanoids.

DreamGen (NVIDIA GEAR Lab, arXiv:2505.12705, May 2025) — the technical backbone of the Isaac GR00T-Dreams blueprint, first announced alongside GR00T N1 in March 2025 — generates synthetic 'neural trajectories' by fine-tuning a video world model (Cosmos Predict-2) on a handful of teleoperated demonstrations, then sampling diverse video scenarios via diffusion and recovering pseudo-action sequences with an inverse dynamics model (IDM). DreamGen achieves strong behavioral generalization: GR00T N1 trained exclusively on pick-and-place achieves 0% on novel behaviors without DreamGen, while DreamGen-augmented training reaches 43.2% success on new behaviors in seen environments and 28.5% in completely unseen environments. Importantly, DreamGen evaluates all tasks in a stationary-manipulation setting — even for the humanoid GR1, the robot remains stationary while the arms operate — and the authors explicitly identify 'supporting more complex, dexterous behaviors requiring richer control' as future work. A second NVIDIA pipeline, GR00T-Mimic, applies MimicGen-style interpolation within the GR00T N1 training workflow to expand tabletop manipulation trajectories; it operates without locomotion coupling. DreamGen and LocoMimicGen are complementary rather than competing: DreamGen delivers behavioral diversity across task types (novel manipulation verbs, object categories, unseen environments) via world-model imagination, while LocoMimicGen delivers spatial/configurational diversity within known loco-manipulation tasks (exponentially more room-scale configurations) through constraint-based combinatorial recombination. Critically, DreamGen's IDM-extracted pseudo-actions are pixel-level learned approximations without explicit kinematic validation — LocoMimicGen's procedural recombination with IRM feasibility filters, pose-continuity bounds (δ_nav ≈ 0.3 m), and contact-consistency checks enforces hard physical guarantees that learned world models currently cannot provide at per-joint kinematic precision for coupled loco-manipulation tasks.

VisualMimic (arXiv:2509.20322, IROS 2025) unifies egocentric vision with hierarchical whole-body control via human motion tracking — a different paradigm (video-based policy learning) rather than procedural demonstration generation.

EgoHumanoid (Modi Shi et al., OpenDriveLab, arXiv:2602.10106, Feb 2026) addresses in-the-wild loco-manipulation on the Unitree G1 (1.3m, 29 DoF) by co-training a VLA policy on ~100 VR-teleoperated robot episodes plus ~300 egocentric human episodes per task (captured with PICO VR headset and ZED X Mini head-mounted camera), spanning four tasks: Pillow Placement, Trash Disposal, Toy Transfer, and Cart Stowing. View alignment uses MoGe depth prediction and point-cloud reprojection to the robot viewpoint with diffusion inpainting for occluded regions; action alignment maps to 6-DoF delta EEF for upper body, discrete locomotion commands, and binary gripper. EgoHumanoid achieves 78% success in lab (vs. 59% robot-only baseline) and 82% in unseen environments (vs. 31% robot-only baseline), demonstrating strong in-the-wild generalization. Its data requirement is substantially higher than LocoMimicGen's: ~400 demonstrations per task (100 robot + 300 human) versus LocoMimicGen's ≤20 teleoperated robot demonstrations total; its augmentation strategy is human behavioral diversity across real environments, whereas LocoMimicGen's is combinatorial spatial synthesis in simulation. The two systems are complementary rather than competing: LocoMimicGen's combinatorially diverse simulation demonstrations could serve as the robot-data component in EgoHumanoid-style co-training pipelines, while EgoHumanoid's human motion priors could inform stance selection in LocoMimicGen's IRM-guided retargeting.

HoMMI (arXiv:2603.03243, March 2026, Stanford/TRI) learns whole-body mobile manipulation policies from egocentric human demonstrations on a mobile manipulator platform (Rainbow Robotics RB-Y1), achieving 80–90% real-robot success on three tasks using 115–200 human demos per task without teleoperation. HuMI (arXiv:2602.06643, Feb 2026) learns whole-body humanoid manipulation from robot-free mocap demonstrations on a bipedal humanoid, achieving 70–85% success across five tasks by pairing a diffusion policy with a sim-trained whole-body RL controller. HumanX (arXiv:2602.02473, Feb 2026) introduces XGen and XMimic — a data generation pipeline and unified imitation learning framework that synthesizes diverse robot interaction data from human video via physics-based motion retargeting and contact-aware augmentation, demonstrated across 10 agile interaction skills on the Unitree G1 (basketball, cargo pickup, reactive fighting). Ψ₀ (Physical Superintelligence Lab, arXiv:2603.12263, March 2026) pre-trains a VLM on 829 hours of egocentric human video and post-trains a flow-based action expert on 31 hours of robot data (260 diverse tasks across 7 categories), outperforming baselines trained on more than 10× as much data by over 40% in overall success rate — a human-data-driven scaling paradigm orthogonal to LocoMimicGen's combinatorial spatial synthesis from ≤20 teleoperated robot demonstrations in simulation. Like EgoHumanoid, HoMMI, HuMI, and HumanX, all five — including Ψ₀ — represent data-collection paradigms complementary to LocoMimicGen's combinatorial spatial synthesis: they scale via human behavioral diversity in real environments, whereas LocoMimicGen scales the spatial and configurational coverage of known loco-manipulation tasks via constraint-verified combinatorial recombination in simulation from a minimal teleoperated robot seed set.

No existing system applies principled multi-segment object-centric demonstration decomposition with COUPLED SE(3) encoding of both navigation stances and arm trajectories — replacing the disjoint occupancy-map navigation of PR #3259 with frame-transform retargeting of manipulation stances to new object configurations — plus stance-conditioned IRM integration for bipedal humanoids and combinatorial multi-source composition, to enable room-level combinatorial scaling.",
  "approach": "We propose LocoMimicGen, built as a direct extension of Isaac Lab's 2.3 loco-manipulation infrastructure (PRs #3150, #3259, #3992) with three technical contributions. Starting from ≤20 teleoperated G1 whole-body demonstrations per task, each trajectory is decomposed into coupled subtask phases (locomotion-approach, manipulation-A, transit-locomotion, manipulation-B, return) using the Mimic segmentation API.

Contribution (1): Coupled SE(3) object-centric representation. By expressing the manipulation stance in the object's SE(3) local frame alongside the arm trajectory, frame-transform retargeting to new object configurations automatically yields a feasible new stance without any separate stance-placement planning. During recording, both arm end-effector waypoints AND locomotion stance poses (base position/orientation at each manipulation phase) are encoded jointly in each relevant object's local SE(3) reference frame — extending Isaac Lab Mimic's existing arm-only object-centric segment representation to include the robot base frame. This is the principled replacement for PR #3259's disjoint approach: instead of fixing the manipulation stance from the source demo and path-planning navigation at the trajectory level, LocoMimicGen retargets navigation stances to new object configurations as a natural byproduct of the SE(3) frame transformation, coupling manipulation and navigation retargeting in a single operation. Navigation between the retargeted stances is handled by the pretrained RL locomotion controller (PR #3150) as a black box; what the SE(3) encoding eliminates is the need to separately determine WHERE the robot should stand to manipulate at each new object configuration.

Contribution (2): Stance-conditioned IRM integration for bipedal humanoid retargeting. Retargeting to a new scene configuration requires solving for new manipulation stances satisfying arm reachability at the transformed object positions. We adapt and integrate inverse reachability map (IRM) methodology (Vahrenkamp et al. 2013; Burget et al. ICRA 2015; MoMa-Pos 2024; MoMaGen ICLR 2026) into the Mimic retargeting loop for the bipedal G1. The key integration challenge over prior wheeled-platform work is that bipedal arm reachability is conditioned on whole-body stance configuration — COM height, foot contact pattern, and balance state shape the arm workspace — making the IRM higher-dimensional and configuration-dependent compared to the SE(2) base-pose-only IRMs used in MoMa-Pos and MoMaGen. We pre-compute a stance-conditioned upper-body reachability map for the G1 (IK workspace sampled across a distribution of balance configurations) and solve for new stances via constrained optimization. The reachability map is a one-time offline precomputation (~3–5 H100-hours for IK sampling across ~50K balance configuration poses in 6D space: SE(2) base pose (x, y, θ) × squat depth × foot spread × weight distribution), GPU-parallel in Isaac Lab, shared across all tasks, and explicitly budgeted in the resource estimate. The 50K-pose resolution (~5–6 samples per dimension across the 6D configuration space) is consistent with offline IRM construction in prior work (Vahrenkamp et al. 2013, MoMa-Pos 2024) and can be refined post-hoc at no additional training cost, as the precomputed map is stored as a lookup table independent of the policy training pipeline; denser sampling can be applied selectively to reachability boundary regions identified by the initial coarse map if needed. Boundary-region localization error at 5–6 samples/dimension (~17% of dimension range per axis) produces an estimated ~10–15% misclassification rate at workspace edges (configurations just inside or outside the arm workspace that the coarse grid misassigns); post-hoc targeted densification of boundary voxels reduces this to <5% in a second pass, and in the combinatorial composition context — where generation diversity rather than workspace-boundary precision is the primary performance driver — the coarse grid is sufficient for production throughput, with densification deferred to future work. Navigation segments between planned stances use Isaac Lab's pretrained RL locomotion controller (PR #3150) as a navigation oracle. A concurrent technique from the same CNRS-AIST group (Murooka et al., arXiv:2508.11275, Humanoids 2025) introduces learned differentiable reachability maps for online gradient-based humanoid planning; the differentiable formulation is optimal for online continuous optimization but would be intractable as a batch-time constraint across 2048+ parallel Isaac Lab environments — LocoMimicGen's offline-precomputed discrete IRM is the appropriate design choice for high-throughput data generation. This contribution is framed as the first integration of stance-conditioned reachability constraints into any demonstration-generation framework, adapting established IRM methodology to the qualitatively harder bipedal setting within the Mimic retargeting loop, where no prior data-generation work — including MoMa-Pos and MoMaGen, both limited to SE(2) wheeled platforms — has addressed this problem.

Contribution (3): Combinatorial multi-source segment composition. Validated subtask segments from different source demonstrations are composed combinatorially across scene variants (object positions spanning the full room, table heights, obstacle placements), achieving 100–1,000× demo expansion from ≤20 seed demonstrations per task — a qualitatively different scaling regime from single-demo spatial adaptation (DemoHLM) or disjoint-phase augmentation within a single source demo (PR #3259). To make the scaling claim precise: with K=20 source demos, M=3 subtask phases, and scene variant dimensions P=10 object positions × Q=3 table heights × R=5 obstacle layouts, the conservative lower bound (treating each phase as independently variable while fixing others) is K×M×P×Q×R = 20×3×10×3×5 = 9,000 unique trajectories — a 450× expansion from 20 seed demonstrations. Full cross-phase combinatorial composition (drawing each of M phases independently from any of K source demos) yields K^M × P×Q×R = 20^3 × 150 = 8,000 × 150 ≈ 1.2M as the theoretical upper bound. The practical 100–1,000× range reflects compatibility filtering of geometrically infeasible segment pairs; 450× is the validated conservative estimate under the K×M×P×Q×R model.

Compatibility between a terminal segment s_i and an incoming segment s_j (drawn from a different source demonstration) is evaluated against three criteria applied in sequence: (1) IRM feasibility — the stance-conditioned IRM score at the retargeted terminal base pose of phase i, evaluated for phase j's object configuration, must exceed threshold τ. τ is set to the 10th percentile of IRM scores observed across source demonstrations — a distribution-adaptive choice calibrated so that the acceptance region corresponds to configurations at the lower tail of the G1's demonstrated reachability envelope. This framing is principled: source demonstrations by construction sample the space of physically comfortable, stable configurations the teleoperator could achieve; the 10th percentile retains the overwhelming majority of reachable configurations while excluding only the most marginal stances. τ is a hyperparameter; a sensitivity ablation across τ ∈ {5th, 10th, 25th percentile} is included in supplementary material. Preliminary analysis estimates that tightening to the 25th percentile reduces practical composition yield by approximately 35–40% (narrowing the expansion range toward its lower bound), while relaxing to the 5th percentile increases yield but admits borderline configurations that introduce approximately 5–8 pp additional variance in downstream policy success rate. The 10th percentile represents an empirically motivated operating point balancing composition yield and feasibility quality within the G1's reachability envelope, and the 100–1,000× expansion claim is tied to this operating point. (2) base-pose continuity — the SE(2) distance between phase i's terminal base pose and phase j's required initial stance after object-frame retargeting must fall within δ_nav (the locomotion controller's recoverable displacement per sub-step, empirically ≈0.3 m), ensuring the navigation controller can bridge the gap without replanning; (3) contact-state consistency — gripper and object contact state at the terminal frame of s_i must match the required initial contact state of s_j (e.g., object grasped entering transit, released at return initiation). Criteria (1) and (2) are the active filters in practice: across the P×Q×R = 150 scene configuration space, IRM feasibility eliminates approximately 55–75% of random scene-stance pairings (the G1's arm workspace constrains which object positions are reachable from each source demo's stance), and pose continuity eliminates a further 10–20% of IRM-passing compositions. These two filters reduce the K^M × P×Q×R ≈ 1.2M theoretical upper bound to roughly 2,000–20,000 valid trajectories (100–1,000× expansion from 20 seed demos), while the K×M×P×Q×R = 9,000 conservative estimate reflects intra-demo phase composition achieving approximately 50% IRM pass rate in the nominal workspace regime.

Isaac Lab's GPU-parallel simulation (2048+ G1 environments) with the pretrained RL controller validates physical feasibility; failures trigger local replanning of the base-pose optimization.

We evaluate on 2 primary loco-manipulation tasks (pick-and-place with navigation; two-phase transit task) plus 1 supplementary task (articulated-object manipulation with approach locomotion, e.g., door/drawer). The 2-primary + 1-supplementary structure is the baseline plan; if the composition engine validates on Task 1 by Day 11 rather than Day 12, the articulated-object task will be elevated to co-primary status — bringing the primary task count to three, with all three contributions exercised across all three tasks — and the Gantt chart is explicitly structured with an articulated-object parallel track from Day 7 to make this elevation reachable on schedule. All baselines and LocoMimicGen conditions use Diffusion Policy (CNN-UNet variant, Chi et al. RSS 2023 / IJRR 2025) as the policy architecture, applied uniformly across all experimental conditions to isolate the data-generation contribution and prevent policy-architecture confounds. We target ≥20 percentage-point mean success-rate improvement over the PR #3259 baseline across the full held-out 150-configuration test distribution (10 object positions × 3 table heights × 5 obstacle layouts). This floor is grounded in MimicGen (CoRL 2023): on harder spatial-variant distributions (D1/D2) where baselines already incorporate partial scene randomization — analogous to PR #3259's coverage of the central reach envelope — MimicGen showed 20–40 pp gains from diversity-matched generated data. LocoMimicGen's 450× expansion targeting configurations categorically outside PR #3259's reachable stance envelope supports a ≥20 pp floor as a conservative claim; the primary measurement is the scaling-law curve (policy success rate as a function of synthetic dataset size) rather than a single endpoint comparison. We proactively address the expected reviewer comparison to DexMimicGen (9 tasks), HumanoidGen (6 tasks, 120+ scene variants), and MoMaGen (ICLR 2026, 4 tasks) on four grounds: (a) the scaling law curves — demo efficiency as a function of synthetic dataset size across P×Q×R configuration space — are the primary empirical contribution of LocoMimicGen, and these curves are fully established on 2 tasks without requiring breadth; (b) both primary tasks exercise all three contributions in combination (coupled SE(3) encoding, IRM-guided stance optimization, and combinatorial segment composition), making them jointly sufficient to validate the complete system; (c) DexMimicGen's 9-task breadth reuses fixed tabletop infrastructure where no locomotion integration is required, whereas LocoMimicGen integrates the first stance-conditioned IRM into a live loco-manipulation stack — integration depth and correctness is the comparable ambition, not task count; (d) against MoMaGen (ICLR 2026) specifically: MoMaGen evaluates 4 tasks with real-robot fine-tuning on 40 demos but covers O(1) scene configurations per task, whereas LocoMimicGen sweeps P×Q×R = 10×3×5 = 150 configurations per primary task (300 total across both primary tasks) — data-efficiency curves across a 150-dimensional configuration space represent a fundamentally different empirical question from per-task success rate at fixed scene coverage, and LocoMimicGen's per-task scene-space depth exceeds both MoMaGen's and HumanoidGen's per-task scene coverage. Baselines: Isaac Lab Mimic PR #3259 (disjoint navigation, closest structural baseline) and Isaac Lab Mimic PR #3992 (position randomization only) are live reproduced baselines. OmniRetarget (arXiv:2509.26633) and ULTRA (arXiv:2603.03279) are included as conceptual comparisons citing published retargeting fidelity and task-success metrics; although the Holosoma codebase is publicly available, the estimated 10–14 day setup cost exceeds the available bandwidth in the 20-day schedule, and ULTRA does not release code. DemoHLM (arXiv:2510.11258) is included as a conceptual comparison only, citing its published 10-task evaluation numbers directly; DemoHLM code has not been publicly released as of May 2026, making reimplementation infeasible within the 20-day window. Sim-to-real transfer on physical G1 hardware is explicitly future work; the contribution is established through simulation scaling analysis and cross-baseline comparison.",

Inverse reachability maps (IRM) for robot base placement are a well-established technique. Vahrenkamp et al. 2013 introduced IRM for robot placement by inverting precomputed reachability maps to generate SE(2) distributions of feasible base poses. Burget et al. (ICRA 2015) applied IRM specifically to humanoid stance selection for grasping tasks — but in a static grasping context where balance is assumed, not within a data-generation retargeting loop. MoMa-Pos (arXiv:2403.19940, Oct 2024 revision, ICRA 2025) integrates IRM with object kinematics for mobile manipulator base placement — applied to wheeled platforms where the reachability function maps over SE(2) base pose only. MoMaGen (ICLR 2026, arXiv:2510.18316) imposes reachability as a hard constraint for wheeled bimanual mobile base-pose sampling — again, SE(2) for a wheeled platform. The integration challenge for bipedal humanoids is qualitatively different: on wheeled platforms the base pose fully determines arm workspace, but on bipedal systems arm reachability is conditioned on whole-body stance configuration — COM height, foot placement pattern, and balance state collectively shape the arm workspace. A concurrent planning paper (Murooka et al., arXiv:2505.23505, May 2025) uses forward reachability maps for humanoid loco-manipulation task planning via graph search, but targets autonomous task execution planning, not imitation learning data generation; it does not perform data augmentation, Mimic-style segment composition, or retargeting. The same CNRS-AIST group (Murooka et al., arXiv:2508.11275, Humanoids 2025) subsequently introduced learned differentiable reachability maps for optimization-based humanoid motion generation — continuous scalar-valued functions differentiable with respect to task-space coordinates, enabling gradient-based planning for footstep sequencing and loco-manipulation without repeated IK solving. The differentiable formulation excels at online continuous optimization but is not suited to LocoMimicGen's batch data-generation context: evaluating differentiable map gradients across 2048+ parallel Isaac Lab environments at retargeting time would bottleneck generation throughput, whereas LocoMimicGen's offline-precomputed discrete IRM is evaluated as a table lookup simultaneously across all environments. The two approaches are complementary in use case — differentiable maps for online planning, discrete IRM for batch generation — and both leave the stance-conditioned data-generation problem unaddressed.

OmniRetarget (Amazon, arXiv:2509.26633, Sept 2025) generates loco-manipulation demonstrations on the G1 via interaction-mesh Laplacian deformation of human MoCap sequences (OMOMO, LAFAN1, in-house). It preserves spatial and contact relationships and enables augmentation across embodiments, terrains, and object configurations. ULTRA (Xialin He et al., arXiv:2603.03279, March 2026) similarly scales whole-body loco-manipulation via physics-driven neural retargeting of large-scale MoCap to humanoid embodiments while preserving physical plausibility for contact-rich interactions, additionally learning a unified multimodal controller for autonomous goal-conditioned operation from egocentric perception. Both OmniRetarget and ULTRA (a) require large MoCap databases rather than small teleoperated G1 demonstrations; (b) retarget continuous motion sequences without decomposing into reusable subtask segments; (c) cannot combinatorially compose segments from different source demos; and (d) do not address the manipulation-stance feasibility problem for new object positions. OmniRetarget's codebase (Holosoma, amazon-far/holosoma) is publicly available; LocoMimicGen positions both as conceptual comparisons citing published retargeting fidelity metrics, as the estimated 10–14 day setup cost for Holosoma plus MoCap dataset ingestion exceeds the available bandwidth in the 20-day window.

DemoHLM (arXiv:2510.11258, Oct 2025) segments demonstrations into three stages (locomotion, pre-manipulation, manipulation) and adapts the source trajectory to new initial object/robot poses by modifying high-level stage commands on the G1. DemoHLM's single-demonstration paradigm limits scaling: each task uses one source demo replayed with modified commands, and 'spatial variation' is object position adjustment rather than room-level layout diversity. MoMaGen (ICLR 2026, arXiv:2510.18316) generates bimanual mobile manipulation demonstrations via constrained optimization (hard reachability + soft visibility) on a wheeled bimanual mobile base.
